's a long-winded explanation, but it boils down to this: when you apply force to something, that force is distributed over an area. Pressure is simply the force per unit area. The pressure experienced at any given point is the sum of all forces applied at that point, divided by the area over which those forces are distributed.

So, if you apply more force to the same area, you'll experience greater pressure. If you apply the same force over a larger area, the pressure will be lower. This is why, for example, a sharp knife (small area) can cut through something more easily than a dull one (larger area) - the force of the cut is concentrated over a smaller area, resulting in higher pressure.

It's also worth noting that pressure isn't just about the force applied externally. Internal forces, such as those arising from molecular interactions within a material, also contribute to the overall pressure experienced at a given point. This is why, for instance, a gas exerts pressure on the walls of its container even though no external force is being applied. The pressure in this case is due to the collisions of the gas molecules with the container walls, which transfer momentum and create a force that is distributed over the area of the container's surface.

In summary, pressure is a measure of the force per unit area experienced at a given point, taking into account both external forces applied and internal forces arising from molecular interactions within a material.
